availability.description: WHEN YOU ARE FREE, and every part of it has a default, so send only what the person said: {"timezone": "America/Chicago", "slot_minutes": 30, "buffer_minutes": 0, "lead_minutes": 120, "max_per_day": 8, "days": 14, "windows": [{"weekday": 1, "from": "09:00", "to": "17:00", "member_user_id": null}]}. `weekday` is 0 for Sunday and 6 for Saturday; `lead_minutes` is how much notice you need; `max_per_day` caps how many appointments a day is offered; `member_user_id` books that window with one named member of the organization. Left out entirely: weekdays 09:00-17:00 UTC, 30-minute slots, two hours' notice, eight a day, fourteen days ahead.

fields.description: What you ask the person, AS FIELDS, created with the table, in the order they are asked: [{"name": "full name", "type": "text", "required": true}, {"name": "email", "type": "email", "required": true}]. Their name and a way to reach them is the minimum — it is what Calendly and Cal.com ask. Do NOT add a field for the time: the page holds and stamps that itself.

home.description: Where a NEW table lives — a home's name or id. Left out, the default home.

intro.description: A line under the page's name, before the times.

notify.description: Who hears about each booking, and about every move and cancellation. `true` (the default) tells the person you are acting for, in the app. {"channel": "email"|"sms"|"in_app", "recipient_user_id": "…"} names a channel and a person. `false` tells nobody.

publish.description: True (the default) opens the page and returns its public link. False leaves it a draft, and the answer says so instead of handing over a link that refuses.

questions.description: Rarely needed — ask only SOME of the table's fields, or in a different order: [{"field": "<field key>", "ask": "…", "help": "…", "required": true}].

submission_cap.description: Stop taking appointments after this many. Left out, there is no cap.

submit_label.description: The confirm button's words, e.g. "Book my consult".

table.description: The name of a NEW table the bookings land in, made with the page. Leave it out and pass table_id instead when the table already exists.

table_id.description: An EXISTING table the bookings land in. Leave it out when you pass `table`.

thank_you.description: The screen after it is booked: {"title": "You're booked", "body": "…"}.

title.description: What the page calls itself on screen, e.g. "Book a 30-minute consult".

booking_propose.how:
A WAY FOR PEOPLE TO BOOK TIME, whole, in ONE call. When somebody asks to let clients book, schedule, make an appointment, reserve a slot or pick a time, that is booking_propose — never a form with a date field, which would take two answers for one eleven o'clock. It makes the table, the questions, the hours, the slots table whose unique index refuses a double-booking, and the published link:
{"action": "booking_propose", "title": "Book a 30-minute consult", "table": "Consults", "fields": [{"name": "full name", "type": "text", "required": true}, {"name": "email", "type": "email", "required": true}], "availability": {"timezone": "America/Chicago", "slot_minutes": 30}, "notify": true}.
Do NOT add a field for the time — the page holds the slot and stamps it on the booking itself. Every part of `availability` has a default, so send only what the person actually said. Each booking is an ordinary record in that table, so you can read, move and cancel it with the other verbs afterwards.

fields.description: What the crew captures, AS FIELDS, in the order they are asked. Each entry is {"name": "weight", "type": "currency"|"number"|"text"|"attachment"|…, "required": true, "ask": "What does it weigh?", "help": "off the scale"}. Use type "attachment" for a photograph or a voice note — that is what makes the phone open a camera or a microphone instead of a text box. A field the AGENT should fill instead carries {"fill": "read the weight off the photo"} and is never asked of the person holding the phone.

home.description: Where a NEW table lives — a home's name or id. Left out, the default home.

intro.description: A line under the sheet's name, before the first question.

notify.description: Who hears about each capture. Left out, nobody — a crew logging two hundred bins a day should not send two hundred notifications. `true`, or {"channel": "email"|"sms"|"in_app", "recipient_user_id": "…"}, turns them on.

open_to_crew.description: True (the default) opens the sheet to the crew and returns the link they open. False leaves it closed, and the answer says so instead of handing over a link that refuses.

questions.description: Rarely needed — ask only SOME of the table's fields, or in a different order: [{"field": "<field key>", "ask": "…", "help": "…", "required": true}].

table.description: The name of a NEW table the captures land in, made with the sheet. Leave it out and pass table_id instead when the table already exists.

table_id.description: An EXISTING table the captures land in. Leave it out when you pass `table`.

thank_you.description: The screen after the last answer: {"title": "Logged", "body": "…"}.

title.description: What the sheet calls itself on the phone, e.g. "Bin round".

capture_propose.how:
A CREW OUT IN THE FIELD, IN ONE CALL. When somebody says their people are ON SITE — photographing something, weighing it, reading a meter, inspecting a property, counting stock in a warehouse — and want it logged where they stand, that is capture_propose, never form_propose. A form is answered by a stranger with a link; a capture sheet is answered by THEIR OWN crew on a phone, often with no signal, and it keeps working: each capture waits on the phone and lands when the bars come back, once, however many times it retries. Give a photograph or a voice note the type attachment — that is what opens the camera and the microphone instead of a text box — and give the agent the columns it can work out for itself:
{"action": "capture_propose", "title": "Bin round", "table": "Bins", "fields": [{"name": "bin id", "type": "text", "required": true, "ask": "Which bin is this?"}, {"name": "weight", "type": "number", "unit": "kg", "required": true, "ask": "What does it weigh?"}, {"name": "photo", "type": "attachment", "required": true, "ask": "Photograph the bin"}, {"name": "voice note", "type": "attachment", "ask": "Anything worth saying?"}, {"name": "contents", "fill": "classify what is in the bin from the photograph"}]}.
It answers with the link the crew opens on their phones. A field carrying `fill` is never asked of the person holding the phone — the agent fills it from what they captured, and that cell says on its face that a model wrote it.

checklist_id.description: Change the checklist that already exists instead of making a second one. The whole thing is re-stated, so send every step, not only the changed one — that is what makes "actually, the laptop should be due on day five" one call.

fields.description: The columns of a NEW table, created with it, in the usual field shape: [{"name": "start date", "type": "date"}]. Ignored with an existing table_id.

home.description: Where a NEW table lives. Left out, the usual Home is used.

name.description: What the checklist is called, e.g. "New hire onboarding".

roles.description: Who does each kind of step: [{"role": "hr", "label": "HR", "user_id": "…"}]. A role with no `user_id` is fine — its steps are created unassigned and the answer says how many are waiting for somebody to be chosen. Any role a step names and this list does not is added here, empty, rather than refused.

start_for.description: Run it once, now, for this record id — so the answer carries a real checklist with real dates and real people rather than a promise of one.

steps.description: The job, in the order it is done, as the person described it. Each step is {"title": "Order the laptop", "role": "it", "due_days": 2, "after": ["Send the contract"], "requires": {"kind": "answer", "key": "serial_number"}}. `role` says WHO does it (a word, matched to `roles` below); `due_days` is how many days after the run starts it is due; `after` names steps that must be finished first, by title or by ref, and may only name steps LISTED ABOVE it; `requires` is what it needs before it counts as done — one of none, note (a sentence of what you did), answer (a named value, with `key`), record_field (a field filled in on the record the run is about), form (with `form_id`) or document (with `template_id`).

table.description: The name of a NEW table the runs are about — People, Hires, Matters — made with the checklist. Leave it out and pass table_id when it already exists.

table_id.description: An EXISTING table the runs are about: one run per record of it. Leave it out when you pass `table`.

trigger.description: What starts a run. "record_created" (the usual one — a new hire arrives), {"kind": "status_reached", "status": "Signed"}, or "manual". Defaults to record_created on the table the checklist is about.

checklist_propose.how:
A PROCESS, whole, in ONE call. When somebody describes how a job is done — "every new hire gets these twelve steps", an onboarding, an SOP, a closing checklist, a what-happens-when — that is checklist_propose. Write down what they SAID, in their order and their words; do not ask them to number it. Each step carries who does it, how many days it has, what it waits for and what it needs before it counts as done:
{"action": "checklist_propose", "name": "New hire onboarding", "table": "Hires", "roles": [{"role": "hr", "user_id": "<id>"}, {"role": "it", "user_id": "<id>"}], "trigger": "record_created", "steps": [{"title": "Send the contract", "role": "hr", "due_days": 0, "requires": {"kind": "note"}}, {"title": "Order the laptop", "role": "it", "due_days": 2, "after": ["Send the contract"], "requires": {"kind": "answer", "key": "serial_number"}}]}.
Every step becomes a real piece of work in somebody's inbox with a real date the moment a record arrives in that table — nobody has to remember to start it. A second sentence like "actually the laptop should be due on day five" is the same call again with checklist_id and the whole list of steps. Pass start_for with a record id to run it once now, so the person sees a real checklist rather than a promise of one.

blocks.description: THE HEART OF IT — the question broken into panels, all of them in this one call. "Jobs by stage this month and what is stuck" is two blocks: [{"title": "Jobs by stage", "kind": "column", "group_by": ["stage"], "measures": [{"op": "count"}], "filter": {"created_at": {"from": "2026-09-01", "to": "2026-10-01"}}}, {"title": "Stuck jobs", "kind": "stuck", "state_key": "stage", "days": 14}]. `kind` is one of number, bar, column, line, donut, table, stuck. `group_by` is a list of field keys; `measures` is [{"op": "count"}] or {"op": "sum"|"avg"|"min"|"max", "key": "<field key>"}; `bucket` is {"key": "created_at", "by": "month"} for a line over time; `filter` takes a plain value for an equality and {"from": …, "to": …} for a half-open moment window (from included, to excluded). A `stuck` block also needs `state_key` (the field that is supposed to move) and `days`. created_at and updated_at are always available; every other key must be a real field of that table.

dashboard_id.description: RE-STATE an existing dashboard instead of making a new one — this is what a follow-up like "now break it down by owner" uses. Send the WHOLE list of blocks you want it to have: the document is replaced, not patched, so a block you leave out is gone.

fields.description: Only when you are making a NEW table with `table`: its fields, the same shape table_propose takes — {"name": "day rate", "type": "currency", "unit": "USD"}. Leave it out for an existing table_id; the dashboard reads that table's own field keys.

home.description: Where a NEW table lives — a home's name or id. Left out, the default home.

name.description: What the dashboard is called — what a person clicks to come back to it, e.g. "Jobs this month".

presentation.description: Rarely needed — how the canvas itself is shown, e.g. {"columns": 12, "description": "Operations, daily"}. Sensible defaults are used without it.

table.description: The name of a NEW table the dashboard is about, made with it. Leave it out and pass table_id instead when the table already exists.

table_id.description: An EXISTING table the dashboard is about — the table most of its blocks ask about. Leave it out when you pass `table`.

dashboard_propose.how:
A QUESTION ABOUT THE WHOLE TABLE, answered as a SCREEN and with the numbers, in ONE call. When somebody asks to see how things stand — a breakdown, a dashboard, what is stuck, how many by stage, a chart of the month — that is dashboard_propose: each part of the sentence becomes a block, it saves them together as a canvas they can open again, and it answers with the rows so you can say the numbers in this same turn. "Show me jobs by stage this month and what's stuck" is:
{"action": "dashboard_propose", "name": "Jobs this month", "table_id": "<id>", "blocks": [{"title": "Jobs by stage", "kind": "column", "group_by": ["stage"], "measures": [{"op": "count"}], "filter": {"created_at": {"from": "2026-09-01", "to": "2026-10-01"}}}, {"title": "Stuck jobs", "kind": "stuck", "state_key": "stage", "days": 14}]}.
`kind` is number, bar, column, line, donut, table or stuck; a filter value that is a plain value is an equality and {"from": …, "to": …} is a moment window (from included, to excluded); created_at and updated_at are always filterable and bucketable, and every other key must be a real field of that table. Pass `table` and `fields` instead of table_id to make the table with the dashboard, and `dashboard_id` to re-state one you already made — a follow-up like "break it down by owner" sends the whole block list again.

body.description: THE DOCUMENT ITSELF, in Markdown, with a column merged in wherever you write {{field:<the column's name>}}. "Dear {{field:client_name}}, for the work at {{field:site_address}} we propose {{field:quoted_total}}, starting {{field:start_date}}." The name is the column's key or its display label, in any casing — both are resolved. Do NOT write the letterhead, the company name, the logo or the address: they are put at the top for you. Do NOT invent a column; the answer's `fields` is every column this table has.

description.description: What a NEW table is for.

fields.description: Only when you are making a NEW table with `table`: its fields, the same shape table_propose takes — {"name": "quoted total", "type": "currency", "unit": "USD"}. Leave it out for an existing table_id.

home.description: Where a NEW table lives — a home's name or id. Left out, the default home.

letterhead.description: True (the default) puts this organization's own letterhead at the top — its name, logo and website, from its settings, never invented. False leaves the document as the wording alone, which is what an internal note wants.

record_id.description: Render THIS record into a document straight away and answer with its link. Leave it out to save the wording without making a document yet.

table.description: The name of a NEW table the document is written for, made with it. Leave it out and pass table_id instead when the table already exists.

table_id.description: The EXISTING table whose records this document is written for. Leave it out when you pass `table`.

template_id.description: RE-WRITE an existing template instead of making a new one — what a follow-up like "add the payment terms" uses. Send the WHOLE body you want it to have; it is replaced, not patched, and every save is a new version because a signature is a seal over one version.

title.description: What this wording is called, e.g. "Job proposal" or "Invoice".

document_propose.how:
A DOCUMENT FROM A RECORD, whole, in ONE call. When somebody asks to turn a row into a proposal, a quote, an invoice, a contract, a letter or a report — "turn this job into a proposal with our letterhead" — that is document_propose. You write the wording and name the columns in the same words a person uses; it resolves them to the Table's real Fields, puts the organization's own letterhead at the top, saves the wording and renders the record, and answers with a link that opens the document with print and save-as-PDF on it:
{"action": "document_propose", "title": "Job proposal", "table_id": "<id>", "record_id": "<the job's id>", "body": "Dear {{field:client_name}},\n\nFor the work at {{field:site_address}} we propose {{field:quoted_total}}, starting {{field:start_date}}."}.
NEVER WRITE THE LETTERHEAD YOURSELF — not the company name, not the logo, not the address. It is put at the top from this organization's own settings, and the answer says in `letterhead.source` where it came from; inventing one would put a company's name on a document it never agreed to. Never invent a column either: a token naming no column is REFUSED and nothing is written, the answer lists every column this table really has in `fields`, and `fix` says exactly what to send — so fix the one token and call again. `template_id` re-writes wording you already saved (send the whole body; every save is a new version), and leaving out `record_id` saves the wording without making a document yet.

columns.description: The columns a model should fill in. Each is {"name": "Industry", "instruction": "the industry this company is in, in two or three words", "type": "text", "inputs": ["title", "website"], "review_interval_days": 30}. `instruction` is in PLAIN WORDS — it is what the model is asked, so write it the way you would say it to a person. `inputs` are OTHER columns of the same record the instruction may read; leave it out and the model gets only what it can look up. `review_interval_days` is how often each value is looked at again; leave it out to fill the column once and never re-check it. `type` is one of the field types (text, number, currency, select, url, …) and defaults to text.

description.description: What a NEW table is for, in one line.

enable.description: Turn the columns on. Turning one on is what authorises the agent to write into it, and it is recorded against the person doing it. False sets it up and writes nothing, which is what to do when somebody wants to look first.

home.description: Where a NEW table lives — a home's name or id.

preview_only.description: Do everything except write: same rows, same model, same cost, and the answer says what WOULD go in each cell. This is what to use when somebody asks to see it on a few rows before turning it on.

rows.description: How many records the first run covers. The organization's own batch ceiling trims a larger ask and the answer says it did.

run.description: Fill in the first batch now. False defines the columns and leaves the filling to the schedule or to somebody pressing the button.

table.description: The name of a NEW table these columns belong to, made with them. Leave it out and pass table_id instead when the table already exists.

table_id.description: The table that already exists, by id.

enrich_propose.how: A COLUMN A MODEL OWNS, AND KEEPS RIGHT — set up AND filled in, in ONE call. *"Fill in each company's industry and headcount, and keep it fresh."* That one sentence names two columns, the instruction for each, a freshness rule and a first run. This action does all of it and answers with the values that actually landed and what they cost, not with a promise. HOW A FILLED-IN VALUE IS DIFFERENT FROM A TYPED ONE, and it matters for what you tell the person afterwards: * every value says on the cell that an AGENT wrote it, for the person who turned the column on, with the model, its version and what it read * an answer the model is not sure enough about is kept as a ranked CANDIDATE and the cell reads "conflicting" — it is never written as if it were a fact * a value past its freshness date is marked STALE and left alone until it is refilled * the moment anybody types over one of these cells, that cell is THEIRS: the next run leaves it exactly as they left it until they hand it back WHAT NOT TO DO. Do not set an enrichment up on a column somebody already types into by hand unless they asked for it — every one of their answers would be pinned on first edit, but the empty ones would be filled in by a model, which is a surprise. And do not ask for a column the answer cannot be worked out from what the record holds plus what the instruction may read: an enrichment with no way to know says "nothing to find" fifty times and charges for it.

entity.description: The standard table's registry token - "party" for a CRM contact or company, "crm_deal" for a deal, "crm_interaction" for a note. Ask for the list rather than guessing one.

record_id.description: The id of the row, from that table.

entity_read.how: ONE STANDARD BUSINESS ROW, WITH THIS ORGANIZATION'S OWN FIELDS ON IT. `record_read` reads a record of one of the organization's OWN tables, by that table's id. This reads a row of a STANDARD table - a CRM contact, a deal, a note, any of the 643 the registry types Entity or Detail - which has no table id at all and is named by its registry TOKEN instead.

entity.description: The standard table's registry token, e.g. "party".

record_id.description: The id of the row to write on.

values.description: The custom fields to set, by their key: {"account_tier": "Gold"}. A key left out is left alone; a key set to null clears that value.

entity_write.how: SET THIS ORGANIZATION'S OWN FIELDS ON ONE STANDARD BUSINESS ROW. A PATCH: a field left out is left alone, and a field set to null is cleared. The definitions BIND - a value outside a choice list, or a word in a money field, is refused in the store's own words rather than written and found later. The row's REAL columns are not touched by this and never can be.

config.description: What a type needs and this tool will not guess: config.via/pick/of/agg/expr for a lookup, rollup or formula; config.kind (date|datetime) for a datetime.

field_type.description: select (one choice from a list Table — REQUIRES options_table_id, the Table the choices are records of) · multi_select (many from the same Table — REQUIRES options_table_id) · member (a person — REQUIRES relation_target) · attachment (a File — REQUIRES relation_target) · lookup (a value read through a relation — REQUIRES config.via and config.pick) · rollup (an aggregate along a relation — REQUIRES config.via, config.of and config.agg) · formula (a declared computation — REQUIRES config.expr, a Rule expression OBJECT, never a sentence) · url · email · phone (text with that format) · currency (a number whose unit is the currency — REQUIRES unit, e.g. USD) · percent · datetime (a date or a date-and-time; config.kind is date or datetime) · checkbox (a REAL true/false; leave the key out and the record stays UNANSWERED, which is a third state and is not false) — plus the plain behaviours text, range, list (REQUIRES options_table_id), relation (REQUIRES relation_target), formula (REQUIRES config.expr), boolean. Anything marked REQUIRES is refused, never guessed — send it on the FIRST call. Aliases: bool→checkbox, boolean→checkbox, choice→select, date→datetime, datetime_local→datetime, decimal→range, dropdown→select, file→attachment, image→attachment, integer→range, link→url, long_text→text, money→currency, multiselect→multi_select, number→range, owner→member, person→member, price→currency, single_select→select, string→text, switch→checkbox, tags→multi_select, tick→checkbox, tickbox→checkbox, timestamp→datetime, toggle→checkbox, user→member, website→url, yes_no→checkbox, yesno→checkbox.

label.description: Display label; defaults to the name.

name.description: The field's human name; its key is derived from it.

options.description: A NEW select/multi_select's choices as words, in order (e.g. ["To do", "In progress", "Done"]); the store makes the Table that holds them. Use this or options_table_id.

options_table_id.description: The table holding the choices of a select/multi_select. Records then store the choice's own word, not that table's row ids.

relation_target.description: The table a relation points at.

table_id.description: The table that gains the field.

unit.description: The unit a currency or percent field carries, e.g. USD.

fields.description: The questions AS FIELDS, created with the table, in the order they are asked. Each entry is {"name": "date of birth", "type": "date", "required": true, "help": "As it appears on your ID"}; `type` is one of the parity field types and defaults to text, `required` makes an answer mandatory, and `ask`/`help` are the form's own wording for that question. Leave this out with an existing table_id and the form asks about every field the table already has.

flow.description: one-at-a-time (Typeform's way, the default) or single-page (Tally's way, better for a short form somebody fills in a hurry).

home.description: Where a NEW table lives — a home's name or id. Left out, the default home.

intro.description: A line under the form's name, before the first question.

notify.description: Who hears about each answer. `true` (the default) tells the person you are acting for, in the app. {"channel": "email"|"sms"|"in_app", "recipient_user_id": "…"} names a channel and a person — email and SMS reach someone only if that address or number is on their account. `false` tells nobody.

publish.description: True (the default) opens the form and returns its public link. False leaves it a draft, and the answer says so instead of handing over a link that refuses.

questions.description: Rarely needed — ask only SOME of the table's fields, or ask them in a different order: [{"field": "<field key>", "ask": "…", "help": "…", "required": true}]. Left out, every field is asked in its own order.

submission_cap.description: Stop accepting after this many answers. Left out, there is no cap.

submit_label.description: The send button's words, e.g. "Send my details".

table.description: The name of a NEW table the answers land in, made with the form. Leave it out and pass table_id instead when the table already exists.

table_id.description: An EXISTING table the answers land in. Leave it out when you pass `table`.

thank_you.description: The screen after the last answer: {"title": "Thanks!", "body": "…"}.

title.description: What the form calls itself on screen, e.g. "New patient intake".

form_propose.how:
A PUBLIC FORM, whole, in ONE call. When somebody asks for a form, an intake, a sign-up sheet, an application or a way for people to send something in, that is form_propose — never a table plus a plan to build a form later. It makes the table, the typed fields, the rule that says what counts as a complete answer, the rule that says who to tell, and the published link, and it answers with that link:
{"action": "form_propose", "title": "New patient intake", "table": "New Patients", "fields": [{"name": "full name", "type": "text", "required": true}, {"name": "date of birth", "type": "date", "required": true}, {"name": "mobile", "type": "phone", "required": true}, {"name": "reason for visit", "type": "text", "help": "In your own words"}], "notify": true}.
Anyone with the link can answer it and nobody can guess it; the answers arrive as ordinary records in that table, stamped with the form they came through. Pass table_id instead of table to put a form on a table that already exists.

csv_text.description: The file's text, with its header row, when you have not parsed it yourself. Use this OR `rows`, never both.

date_order.description: How a slashed date is read: "mdy" for 11/30/2026 or "dmy" for 30/11/2026. Chosen once for the whole file. Ask the person if the file is ambiguous and you cannot tell — reading it wrong is invisible until March.

dedupe_key.description: The column that makes a row the SAME row — an order number, an email, a name. A row whose value for it is already in the table is left alone (or brought up to date) instead of written twice. Ask the person which column it is when the file plainly has one; leave it out and every row is written.

file_hash.description: The sha-256 of the file's bytes, if you have it. It is what makes importing the same file twice write nothing at all. Leave it out rather than inventing one — a wrong hash would make a DIFFERENT file look like this one and skip it.

home.description: Where a NEW table lives, by name. Left out, it goes to the default home.

mapping.description: Rarely needed — the file's heading to the table's column key, when a heading does not match: {"Client": "account"}. Left out, the store matches by name and offers what it could not match.

on_duplicate.description: "skip" leaves the record that is already there; "update" brings it up to date from the file. Only meaningful with dedupe_key.

rows.description: The file's rows, one object per row, keyed by the file's OWN column headings and holding the cell text exactly as the file spells it: [{"Deal": "Roof job", "Amount": "$1,250.00", "Closes": "11/30/2026"}]. Send `csv_text` instead when you are holding the file's text rather than parsed rows.

source_name.description: The file's name, so the records say where they came from. e.g. "deals.csv".

table.description: The name of a NEW table the rows land in, made from the file's own columns. Leave it out and pass table_id when the table already exists.

table_id.description: An EXISTING table the rows land in. Leave it out when you pass `table`.

unmapped.description: What happens to a column the table does not have: "propose" puts it in the approvals inbox for somebody to say yes to (the default, and the only choice somebody who is not an admin of the table has), "create" adds it outright, "ignore" leaves it out. Never silently dropped.

import_propose.how:
A FILE SOMEBODY SENT YOU, IN ONE CALL. When somebody attaches a spreadsheet or a CSV and asks you to pull it in, load it, import it or "put this in a table", that is import_propose. Send the rows EXACTLY as the file spells them — do not convert anything, do not guess a type, do not strip a dollar sign or reformat a date. The store works every column out from the values AND from what this organization already has: money keeps its currency, dates become dates, a few repeating words become a dropdown, an address that belongs to somebody here becomes a person, and names that are all records of another table become a pointer at it. Anything it cannot place goes to the approvals inbox as a new column — never dropped:
{"action": "import_propose", "table": "Deals", "source_name": "deals.csv", "dedupe_key": "deal", "rows": [{"Deal": "Roof job", "Amount": "$1,250.00", "Closes": "11/30/2026", "Stage": "Open", "Account": "Northwind Trading"}]}.
ASK FOR TWO THINGS FIRST when the file plainly has them and you cannot tell: which column makes a row the SAME row (dedupe_key — it is what stops a corrected re-import doubling everything), and, for slashed dates, whether the day or the month comes first. Pass table_id instead of table to add to a table that already exists. THE SAME CALL SAVES ROWS THAT ARE ALREADY IN THE CONVERSATION (Arman, 2026-09-29: one "Save to a table" for every shape): a markdown table in an answer, a list or a few bullet points (one row per item — one "Item" column, or split at a delimiter every item shares), `Key: value` lines (one row, a column per key), the items of a kind value. Turn what the person pointed at into `rows` keyed by the headings or keys exactly as written, and send them here — never a second table-making route. An existing table whose choice column does not know a word refuses that row by name; say which word and offer to add it. The answer says how many landed, how many were already there and how many were refused WITH the reason and the row — say those numbers; never report a count you were not given.

limit.description: How many matches to return at most.

query.description: Text matched against table and field names and descriptions. This searches STRUCTURE, never rows — use record_read or record_aggregate for data.

fields.description: Only when you are making a NEW table with `table`: its fields, the same shape table_propose takes. The stage column is NOT one of them — describe that in `stage_field`.

limits.description: How many cards may sit in a stage at once: {"Proposal": 3}. The card being moved is not counted against the limit.

measure.description: A number column to TOTAL under each column heading, e.g. `amount`. Leave it out and the headings carry counts only.

on_entry.description: What happens when a card ARRIVES in a stage, per stage: {"Won": {"assign": "<a person's id>", "checklist": "<a template id>", "notify": {"user": "<id>", "subject": "…", "body": "…"}}}. Each one goes through the door that already owns it, in the same transaction as the move, so it does not happen when the move is refused.

requires.description: What must be filled in before a card may land in a stage: {"Won": ["signed_proposal"]}. The keys are stage names; the values are column keys of this same table. A person who tries anyway is told which column, by its label, and a screen can offer it to them.

stage_field.description: The column that holds the stage: {"key": "stage", "label": "Stage", "options": ["Lead", "Qualified", "Won"]}. THE OPTIONS ARE THE BOARD'S COLUMNS, IN THE ORDER YOU WRITE THEM. When the column already exists, send just its key.

table.description: The name of a NEW table the board is about, made with it. Leave it out and pass table_id instead when the table already exists.

table_id.description: An EXISTING table the board is about. Leave it out when you pass `table`.

transitions.description: Where a card may go from where it is: [{"from": "Lead", "to": "Qualified"}, …]. Leave it out and every move is allowed. Staying put is always allowed, because most writes to a record are not moves at all.

view_name.description: What the saved board is called. Defaults to the table's name followed by "by" and the stage column's label.

who.description: Who may move a card INTO a stage: {"Won": "admin"}. One of viewer, commenter, editor or admin — a rung on this record, not a job title.

pipeline_propose.how:
A BOARD OF THINGS BY STAGE, WITH THE RULES THAT JUDGE EVERY MOVE, in ONE call. When somebody asks for a pipeline, a board, a kanban, deals by stage, a hiring funnel, tickets by status — anything where things MOVE between named columns — that is pipeline_propose. It makes the Choice column, marks it as the table's stage column, writes each policy as a Rule the store enforces on every write, saves the board and answers with its address AND its live counts:
{"action": "pipeline_propose", "table_id": "<id>", "stage_field": {"key": "stage", "label": "Stage", "options": ["Lead", "Qualified", "Proposal", "Won", "Lost"]}, "transitions": [{"from": "Lead", "to": "Qualified"}, {"from": "Qualified", "to": "Proposal"}, {"from": "Proposal", "to": "Won"}], "requires": {"Won": ["signed_proposal"]}, "who": {"Won": "admin"}, "limits": {"Proposal": 3}, "measure": "amount"}.
THE OPTIONS ARE THE COLUMNS, IN THE ORDER YOU WRITE THEM. A SECOND SENTENCE ADDS A RULE RATHER THAN REBUILDING THE BOARD: "and nothing moves to Won without a signed proposal" is the same verb again with table_id, the same stage_field.key, and nothing but `requires` — what you do not mention is left exactly as it was. The answer carries every rule WITH the sentence it says when it refuses, so warn somebody before they try instead of after. Pass `table` and `fields` instead of table_id to make the table with the board.

client_fields.description: Only when you are making a NEW client table with `client_table`: its fields, the same shape table_propose takes — {"name": "company", "type": "text"}. Left out, the client list is made with a name and an email, which is the least a person needs to be invited. Ignored for an existing client_table_id.

client_table.description: The name of a NEW table whose records ARE the clients — one record per person or company who will sign in. Made with the portal. Leave it out and pass client_table_id instead when that list already exists.

client_table_id.description: An EXISTING table whose records are the clients. Leave it out when you pass `client_table`.

home.description: Where a NEW client table lives — a home's name or id. Left out, the default home.

invite.description: Who to invite right now, one entry per person: [{"client_record_id": "<the client record's id>", "email": "ann@acme.com"}]. `client` is accepted instead of `client_record_id` for the same value. Left out, the portal is made and nobody is invited yet — an invitation can be sent at any time afterwards. An invitation confers nothing on its own: the person gets in only by following their own sign-in link.

tables.description: THE HEART OF IT — every Table the portal shows, and how each one knows whose row is whose, all in this one call: [{"table": "Jobs", "names_via": "client", "visible_fields": ["title", "stage", "scheduled_for"], "editable_fields": [], "comments": true}, {"table": "Invoices", "names_via": "client", "comments": false}]. `table` is a table's name or its id. `names_via` is the field on THAT table that names the client a row belongs to — it must point at the client list, and a field of that name is created as a relation to the client list when it does not exist yet. `visible_fields` is what a signed-in client sees (left out: every field of that table); `editable_fields` is the subset they may change (left out: nothing is editable); `comments` true lets them write a comment on a row (left out: they cannot).

title.description: What the portal calls itself on screen, e.g. "Client portal".

portal_propose.how:
A PORTAL FOR CLIENTS, whole, in ONE call. When somebody asks to let their clients, customers, tenants or students sign in and see only their own rows — their jobs, their invoices, their case — that is portal_propose, never a table plus a plan to build sharing later. It makes the list of clients, the link from every exposed table back to that list, the portal and its address, and it invites the people you name:
{"action": "portal_propose", "title": "Client portal", "client_table": "Clients", "tables": [{"table": "Jobs", "names_via": "client", "visible_fields": ["title", "stage", "scheduled_for"], "comments": true}, {"table": "Invoices", "names_via": "client"}], "invite": [{"client_record_id": "<id>", "email": "ann@acme.com"}]}.
`names_via` is the whole of it: the field on THAT table that names the client a row belongs to, which is the only reason one person sees eleven rows and not two hundred. A field of that name that does not exist yet is created as a relation to the client list, and rows that name nobody are seen by nobody until they do. `visible_fields` left out shows every field; `editable_fields` left out means they can change nothing; `comments` lets them write on a row. Pass client_table_id instead of client_table when the list of clients already exists. An invitation confers nothing on its own — a person sees their rows only after following their own sign-in link.

field_key.description: The field being measured, required for anything but count. Its key or its display label, either works.

group_by.description: Field to bucket by — its key or its display label, either works.

limit.description: How many buckets to return at most.

measure.description: count | sum | avg | min | max, computed inside the query.

undo.description: True restores a record that was deleted before.

field_key.description: Narrow it to one column, by its key — the question people usually ask ("who changed the price?"). Leave it out for the whole record.

limit.description: How many versions to read at most (capped at 500).

record_id.description: The record whose past you want.

id_keyed.description: record_id form only: key the values by field id instead of field name.

limit.description: How many records to return at most.

match.description: Only records whose fields equal these, e.g. {"region": "North"}. Field key or display label, either works.

record_id.description: ONE record, by id. Leave it out when you pass table_id.

table_id.description: Read ALL the records of this table in one call, instead of one record_read per id. Returns a list.

field_key.description: Put back ONE column instead of the whole record, by its key. Everything else on the record is left exactly as it is.

version.description: The version to go back to — a number from record_history. The write is a NEW version; nothing in the record's history is ever erased.

expected_version.description: Opt-in compare-and-swap: a stale write is refused with the contested fields instead of overwriting someone else's change.

record_id.description: Present means PATCH that record; absent means create a new one.

records.description: ALL the records to create, in ONE call, all in the same table. This is the normal way to write more than one record — never call record_write in a loop. Example: {"action": "record_write", "table_id": "<id>", "records": [{"crew_name": "North Crew", "region": "North", "day_rate": 1200}, {"crew_name": "South Crew", "region": "South", "day_rate": 1450}]}. Each entry IS the field map — do not wrap it in `values`. A choice column takes the choice's own WORD, never an id. Up to 200 at a time; one refused row rolls the whole batch back.

table_id.description: The table being written to. Required when creating.

values.description: ONE record as {field key: value}. For more than one record use `records` instead — never call this action in a loop. A CHOICE column takes the choice's own WORD, exactly as the column offers it ("Circle"), never an id; a word that is not one of the choices is refused and the refusal lists them. A multi-choice column takes a list of those words.

expires_days.description: How long the link works. Fourteen days unless you say otherwise.

field.description: The key of the signature column on that record's table: a text column whose format is `signature`. The store names the ones that exist if this is wrong.

record_id.description: The record the document is about — the job, the quote, the case.

render_id.description: A document version that already exists. Use this OR `template_id`.

signer_email.description: Who is being asked, by address. They need no account here.

signer_name.description: Who is being asked, by name. Shown on the signing page so the person opening the link can see they are the one who was meant to.

template_id.description: The document template to render over this record. Use this OR `render_id`, never neither — a signature seals a document VERSION and there is nothing sensible to guess.

signature_request.how:
HAVE THE CLIENT SIGN IT. "Have them sign this before we start" is signature_request, never an attachment and never another vendor: a signature here is a Value ON the record, carrying who signed, when, from what address and browser, and the hash of the exact document version they saw. One call:
{"action": "signature_request", "record_id": "<the job>", "template_id": "<the proposal template>", "field": "client_signature", "signer_email": "dana@acme.com", "signer_name": "Dana Okonkwo"}.
`field` is a signature column on that record’s table — a text column whose format is `signature`; the store names the ones that exist if you get it wrong. It answers with a link, ONCE, because only a fingerprint of it is stored: hand that link to the person, because nothing here emails it for you and saying otherwise would be a lie. The link stops working when it expires, when they sign or decline, or the moment the record changes — nobody signs a document the record no longer supports.

table_id.description: The table to watch. It has to exist — use table_propose or form_propose first if it does not, then subscribe to it.

tell.description: One entry per thing the person asked to be told, in their order: [{"cadence": "instant", "channel": "sms"}, {"cadence": "weekly", "channel": "email", "schedule": "monday 08:00"}]. Each entry may also carry "name", "recipient_user_id" and "quiet_hours" ({"start": "22:00", "end": "07:00", "tz": "America/Chicago"}). channel is in_app, email or sms; left out, in_app. Left out, the recipient is the person the agent is working for.

view_id.description: Subscribe over a saved view that already exists instead of making one. Pass this OR `watch`, never both.

view_name.description: What to call the saved view this makes, in the person's words — "New leads". It is what they will see and edit when they want to change what counts. Left out, the table's name and the filter.

watch.description: WHAT COUNTS, as a filter on that table's own field keys: {"stage": "new"} is "a new lead". Every key has to be a real field key of that table. Left out, everything in the table counts, and the answer says so.

subscription_propose.how:
BEING TOLD WHEN SOMETHING HAPPENS, all of it, in ONE call. When somebody asks to be told, texted, emailed or notified about something — "text me on a new lead; email me a Monday summary" — that is subscription_propose, never two subscriptions assembled by hand over two different filters that then quietly stop agreeing. It writes WHAT COUNTS down once as a saved view the person can edit later in plain English, and one subscription per thing they asked to be told, all over that one view:
{"action": "subscription_propose", "table_id": "<the leads table>", "watch": {"stage": "new"}, "view_name": "New leads", "tell": [{"cadence": "instant", "channel": "sms"}, {"cadence": "weekly", "channel": "email", "schedule": "monday 08:00"}]}.
instant means the moment a record ENTERS that view — a field edit on one already in it sends nothing. A summary names what entered, what left and what changed since the last one, and an empty summary is not sent at all. Quiet hours ({"start": "22:00", "end": "07:00", "tz": "America/Chicago"}) MOVE a message to the moment they end; they never drop it.

limit.description: How many tables to return at most (capped at 500).

fields.description: The table's fields, created with it. Each entry is {"name": "day rate", "type": "currency", "unit": "USD"}; `type` is one of the parity field types and defaults to text. The answer carries every field's key and field_id, so you never have to read the table back.

home.description: Where the table lives — a home's name or id from table_list. Leave it out and this organization's default home is used, and made if there is none.

name.description: The table's human name, e.g. "Field Crews".

spec.description: Rarely needed — overrides for the rest of the table spec (display, weight, retention_days, default_sort…). Sensible defaults are used without it.

unknown.note: '__MATRX_RECORDS_UNKNOWN_GUIDE_TOPIC__' is not an action of this tool. Call {"action": "guide", "topic": "<action>"} with one of these.
